items.title: Panchamahabhuta
items.summary: Ayurveda describes all matter, including the body, food and medicines, as composed of five elements (Mahabhutas). They are categories of qualities, not chemical elements.

p: The elements explain the three doshas (Vata from Space and Air; Pitta from Fire and Water; Kapha from Water and Earth), the six tastes (Rasa) and the actions of foods and drugs. A drug with predominantly Earth and Water, for example, is described as heavy and nourishing.

Panchamahabhuta is a philosophical and qualitative framework from Samkhya and Nyaya-Vaisheshika thought. It does not correspond to chemical elements or to modern physics; it is best read as a system for classifying observable qualities.

items.title: Tridosha
items.summary: The three doshas are the functional principles that govern the body in health and cause disease when disturbed: Vata (movement), Pitta (transformation) and Kapha (structure and cohesion).

head: Dosha
Elements
Qualities (Guna)
Main seat
Governs
rows: Dry, light, cold, rough, subtle, mobile
All movement: breathing, circulation, speech, elimination, nerve function
Slightly oily, sharp, hot, light, fleshy-smelling, flowing, liquid
Digestion, metabolism, body heat, vision, complexion, intellect
Oily, cold, heavy, slow, smooth, slimy, stable

p: Each dosha can be increased (Vriddhi), decreased (Kshaya) or in balance (Samya). Like qualities increase a dosha and opposite qualities reduce it: cold, dry, light food and weather increase Vata; warm, oily, heavy food calms it. This 'like increases like' principle (Samanya-Vishesha) underlies Ayurvedic diet and treatment.

The doshas are an explanatory model of physiology, not anatomical structures or measurable substances. Attempts to correlate them with modern markers (genes, metabolic rate, autonomic function) are an active but preliminary research area. A 'dosha imbalance' is never a substitute for a medical diagnosis.

items.title: Sapta Dhatu and Mala
items.english: The seven tissues and the waste products
items.summary: Dhatus are the seven tissues that support the body, each nourished in turn from the one before. Malas are the waste products of digestion and metabolism.

p: The three main Malas are Purisha (faeces), Mutra (urine) and Sveda (sweat). Each Dhatu also produces its own minor waste (Kitta), such as ear wax, nails and hair in classical descriptions. Proper elimination is considered as important as proper nourishment.

The sequential nourishment of tissues (Rasa to Rakta to Mamsa and so on) is a classical theory of metabolism. Modern physiology describes tissue nutrition through circulation to all tissues simultaneously. English equivalents above are approximate.

items.title: Srotas
items.summary: Srotas are the channels through which doshas, tissues, nutrients and wastes move. Disease begins where a channel is blocked or damaged and a disturbed dosha lodges there.

list: Atipravritti: excessive flow
Sanga: obstruction
Siragranthi: nodular swelling of vessels
Vimargagamana: flow in the wrong direction

p: Sushruta describes eleven pairs of channels, including Artavavaha (menstrual) channels; Manovaha (channels of the mind) is also discussed. Locators and roots above follow the commonly taught Charaka list and should be checked against the edition used in your course.

items.title: Agni
items.summary: Agni is the principle of digestion and transformation. Ayurveda considers weak or irregular Agni to be the root of most disease.

list: Jatharagni (1): the main digestive fire in the stomach and small intestine
Bhutagni (5): one for each element, transforming food into the body's elements
Dhatvagni (7): one for each tissue, governing tissue metabolism

head: State
Description
Associated dosha
rows: Irregular: sometimes strong, sometimes weak; bloating, variable appetite
Sharp: very strong hunger, digests quickly, burning
Weak: slow digestion, heaviness, low appetite

list: Eat when hungry and after the previous meal is digested
Make the midday meal the main meal
Prefer warm, freshly cooked food
Avoid frequent snacking and large late-night meals

p: Agni broadly overlaps with digestive enzymes, gut motility and cellular metabolism, but it is a functional concept rather than a single organ or enzyme. Persistent loss of appetite, weight loss or indigestion needs medical evaluation.

items.title: Ama
items.summary: Ama is the sticky, heavy, poorly digested material produced when Agni is weak. It is said to clog channels and combine with doshas to cause disease.

list: Coated tongue
Heaviness and lethargy
Loss of appetite and taste
Sticky, foul-smelling stools
Generalised aches

p: A dosha mixed with Ama is called Sama; without Ama it is Nirama. Treatment differs: in Sama states, physicians first use fasting or light diet (Langhana) and digestive medicines (Pachana) before nourishing or oily treatments.

Ama has no single modern equivalent. Some researchers relate it to incompletely digested food, gut dysbiosis or inflammatory states, but this is speculative. A coated tongue and heaviness have many causes.

items.title: Ojas
items.summary: Ojas is described as the refined essence of all seven tissues, the basis of strength, immunity and vitality.

p: Charaka describes Ojas as residing in the heart, whitish-yellow and slightly reddish, with the qualities of ghee and honey. Two forms are named: Para Ojas (supreme, very small in quantity) and Apara Ojas (circulating). Ojas is said to be depleted by anger, grief, worry, fasting, overexertion and chronic disease.

list: Ojo Visramsa: displacement, with fatigue and weakness
Ojo Vyapat: vitiation, with heaviness and pallor
Ojo Kshaya: depletion, with fainting, wasting and confusion

p: Ojas is often compared to immunity or overall physiological reserve, but there is no measurable substance corresponding to it. Rasayana measures and good sleep, diet and emotional health are the classical means of preserving Ojas.

items.title: Prakriti and Vikriti
items.summary: Prakriti is a person's inborn constitution, fixed at conception by the predominant doshas. Vikriti is the current, changeable state of imbalance.

list: Single-dosha: Vata, Pitta or Kapha
Dual: Vata-Pitta, Pitta-Kapha, Vata-Kapha
Sama: balanced (considered the best)
The condition of sperm and ovum (Shukra-Shonita)
Season and condition of the uterus
The mother's diet and conduct during pregnancy
The proportions of the elements

p: Charaka describes sixteen mental types grouped by the three qualities of mind: Sattva (clarity), Rajas (activity, passion) and Tamas (inertia).

Questionnaires to assess Prakriti vary, and agreement between assessors is moderate in published studies. Some studies report associations with genetic and metabolic markers, but these are preliminary. Prakriti assessment is a lifestyle guide, not a diagnostic test.

sources.text: Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana 8 and Sharira Sthana 4

items.title: Shat Kriyakala
items.summary: Sushruta describes six stages through which a disturbed dosha becomes a disease. Each stage is an opportunity for treatment; the earlier the intervention, the easier the cure.

head: Stage
Sanskrit
What happens
rows: Accumulation of the dosha in its own seat
Aggravation: the accumulated dosha becomes excited
Spread: the dosha overflows and moves through the body
Localisation: the dosha lodges in a weak tissue or channel; early warning signs (Purvarupa)
Manifestation: the disease appears with its characteristic signs (Rupa)
Differentiation and complication: the disease becomes chronic or specific

p: The model emphasises prevention and early treatment. Modern medicine has a parallel idea in primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, although the mechanisms are described very differently.

items.title: Ayurvedic anatomy (Rachana Sharira)
items.summary: Classical texts include detailed anatomy based on observation, including Sushruta's method of studying a cadaver softened in water. Counts and names often differ from modern anatomy.

p: Sushruta Samhita (Sharira Sthana 5) describes preparing a body by immersion in a river and scraping away layers to observe structures, one of the earliest recorded descriptions of dissection-based study.

head: Structure
Classical count
Modern note
rows: 206 in the adult; classical counts include teeth, nails and cartilages and some separately counted parts
Epidermis has several strata; dermis and hypodermis are separate layers

p: Classical anatomy is historically important and still taught in BAMS (Rachana Sharira), alongside modern anatomy. For clinical decisions, modern anatomy is the standard.

items.title: Marma Sharira
items.summary: Marmas are 107 anatomical sites where muscle, vessels, ligaments, bone and joints meet. Injury to them can cause death, disability or severe pain, according to Sushruta.

head: Type
Number
Effect of injury
rows: Death when a foreign body is removed

list: Mamsa (muscle)
Sira (vessels)
Snayu (ligaments and tendons)
Asthi (bone)
Sandhi (joints)
Upper and lower limbs: 11 in each limb (44)
Chest and abdomen: 12
Back: 14
Head and neck: 37

p: Shiras (head), Hridaya (heart) and Basti (bladder) are called the Trimarma; many diseases are described in relation to them.

Many marmas lie over major vessels, nerves or joints, so the surgical caution they encode is consistent with modern anatomy. Therapeutic 'marma therapy' (pressure or massage at marmas) has very limited clinical evidence.

sources.text: Sushruta Samhita, Sharira Sthana 6 (Pratyeka Marma Nirdesha)

items.title: Nidana Panchaka
items.english: Five means of understanding a disease
items.summary: Classical diagnosis rests on five components that together describe how a disease arises and shows itself. Every condition article in this encyclopedia is organised around them.

head: Component
Meaning
rows: Causes: diet, lifestyle, season, external factors
Early warning signs before the disease is fully expressed
Diagnostic response: what relieves or aggravates (a therapeutic test)
Pathogenesis: how the disturbed dosha travels and lodges

p: Samprapti is summarised by its components (Ghataka): the dosha involved, the tissues affected (Dushya), the channels (Srotas), the type of channel disturbance, the seat of disease (Adhishthana), the state of Agni and whether Ama is present. Condition articles show these in Doctor and Student views.

items.title: Rogi and Roga Pariksha
items.summary: Classical texts describe several structured examination systems. In modern practice they complement, never replace, clinical examination and investigations.

list: Darshana: inspection
Sparshana: palpation
Prashna: history-taking
Nadi: pulse
Mutra: urine
Mala: stool
Jihva: tongue
Shabda: voice and body sounds
Sparsha: touch, temperature, texture
Drik: eyes
Akriti: build and appearance

sections.h: Dashavidha Pariksha (tenfold assessment of the patient)
list: Prakriti: constitution
Vikriti: current disorder
Sara: tissue excellence
Samhanana: compactness of build
Pramana: body measurements
Satmya: habituation, what suits the person
Sattva: mental strength
Ahara Shakti: capacity to take and digest food
Vyayama Shakti: exercise capacity
Vaya: age

p: Pulse reading appears in later texts (Sharangadhara Samhita; Yogaratnakara) rather than in Charaka or Sushruta. Studies of agreement between practitioners and of diagnostic accuracy are few and inconsistent. Pulse reading must not replace blood pressure measurement, ECG, laboratory tests or imaging when these are indicated.

Many classical conditions overlap with diseases that need laboratory confirmation: blood sugar and HbA1c for Prameha/diabetes, haemoglobin for Pandu/anaemia, liver tests for Kamala/jaundice, thyroid tests, urine examination, imaging for stones. Ayurvedic Standard Treatment Guidelines (Ministry of AYUSH) also recommend relevant modern investigations.

items.title: Principles of diet (Ahara)
items.summary: Ayurveda treats food as the first medicine. What, how much, when, where and how one eats are all considered.

sections.h: Eight factors of diet (Ashta Ahara Vidhi Visheshayatana)

head: Factor
Meaning
rows: Natural qualities of the food (heavy, light, hot, cold)
Processing: cooking, soaking, roasting change its qualities
Place of origin and of eating
Time: of day, season, state of digestion
The person who eats: constitution, habit, digestive capacity

list: Eat warm, freshly prepared, slightly unctuous food
Eat the right quantity, after the previous meal is digested
Avoid incompatible combinations
Eat in a pleasant place, without hurry, without talking or laughing excessively
Eat attentively, considering what suits you

p: A classical guideline divides the stomach into thirds: one third solid food, one third liquid, one third left empty for digestion. In modern terms this is advice to stop before feeling full.

Classical principles fit well with balanced modern diets: plenty of vegetables, pulses and whole grains, limited ultra-processed food, sugar and salt. People with diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease, allergies or other medical conditions should follow their clinician's or dietitian's specific advice.

items.title: Shad Rasa
items.summary: Ayurveda classifies foods and medicines by six tastes. Each taste is formed from two elements and affects the doshas in a characteristic way.

head: Taste
Sanskrit
Elements
Effect on doshas
Examples
rows: Reduces Vata and Pitta; increases Kapha
Reduces Vata; increases Pitta and Kapha
Reduces Vata; increases Pitta and Kapha
Reduces Kapha; increases Vata and Pitta
Reduces Pitta and Kapha; increases Vata
Reduces Pitta and Kapha; increases Vata

p: A balanced meal includes all six tastes, weighted toward those that calm the person's predominant dosha. Excess of any one taste is said to cause disorders; for example, excess salt is linked classically to hair greying, wrinkles and bleeding disorders, which aligns with modern advice to limit salt.

items.title: Viruddha Ahara
items.summary: Charaka lists combinations and practices that are considered harmful even if each food is wholesome alone.

list: Milk with fish
Milk with sour fruits or salt
Honey heated or added to very hot food
Honey and ghee in equal quantities
Curd at night, or heated curd
Heavy food after a large meal (eating before digestion)

p: Charaka describes eighteen kinds, including incompatibility of place, time, digestive capacity, dose, habit, dosha, processing, potency, bowel state, health state, order of eating, rules of eating, palatability, combination, richness and the person's mental state.

Most of these rules have not been tested in clinical studies. Some align with modern advice (for example, avoiding very large or late meals). Do not avoid nutritious foods such as milk or fish altogether on these grounds alone, particularly for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Pathya Kalpana
items.summary: Light, easily digested preparations used during illness and recovery, especially after fasting or Panchakarma, in a graded sequence from thin gruel to normal meals.

head: Preparation
Description
rows: Clear liquid strained from rice cooked in much water
Thin rice gruel with a few grains
Gruel, often of rice or barley, sometimes cooked with herbs
Soup of pulses, especially green gram (mung)
Buttermilk: diluted, churned curd with the fat removed

p: After fasting or purification therapy, food is reintroduced gradually from Manda or Peya through Vilepi and Yusha to normal meals over several days, to let digestion recover. The exact sequence is set by the physician.

items.title: Simple healthy recipes
items.summary: Easily digested everyday dishes associated with Ayurvedic cooking. These are household recipes, not treatments.

list: Rinse ½ cup rice and ½ cup split yellow mung dal
Warm 1 tablespoon ghee; add ½ teaspoon cumin seeds, a pinch of asafoetida (hing) and 1 teaspoon grated ginger
Add rice, dal, ½ teaspoon turmeric and 4 cups water; add vegetables if wished
Simmer until soft (about 25–30 minutes, or 3 whistles in a pressure cooker); add salt to taste
Serve warm; finish with coriander leaves
Blend 1 part fresh plain curd (yoghurt) with 3–4 parts water
Add a pinch of roasted cumin powder, a little rock salt and grated ginger
Drink at room temperature with or after lunch
Avoid at night; avoid if you have a cold and congestion
Soak ½ cup whole green gram for 4–6 hours
Cook with 4 cups water until very soft
Temper with ghee, cumin, ginger and a pinch of black pepper
Add salt and a squeeze of lemon; serve thin

p: People with diabetes should be mindful of rice quantity; those with kidney disease should check salt and potassium advice with their doctor; dairy-free versions can use oil instead of ghee.

items.title: Dinacharya
items.summary: A daily routine of waking early, cleansing, oil massage, exercise, regular meals and timely sleep is the foundation of Ayurvedic prevention.

head: Practice
What it involves
rows: Attending to natural urges without straining
Cleaning teeth; classically with twigs of neem, babul or similar bitter-astringent plants
Holding or swishing oil or decoctions in the mouth
Eye care with collyrium (classical; use only safe, approved products)
A drop or two of oil in each nostril
Oil massage, especially of head, ears and feet
Exercise to half of one's capacity (Ardha Shakti), until light sweating
Main meal at midday; light, early dinner
Going to bed at a regular, early hour

list: Traditional kohl and some 'surma' products have been found to contain lead; do not use them, especially for children
Do not use oil nasal drops if you have a cold, sinus infection, or immediately after meals
Adjust exercise for heart, lung or joint conditions and pregnancy with your doctor

p: Regular sleep and meal timing, daily physical activity and oral hygiene are well supported by modern evidence. Tongue scraping can reduce tongue coating and odour; oil pulling has limited, low-quality evidence and does not replace brushing and dental care.

items.title: Ritucharya
items.summary: Diet and conduct change with each of six seasons, because strength, digestion and doshas change through the year.

p: Uttarayana or Adana Kala (late winter, spring, summer): the sun 'takes away' strength; people are weaker by summer. Dakshinayana or Visarga Kala (rains, autumn, early winter): the moon 'gives' strength; people are strongest in early winter.
The two weeks between seasons (the last week of one and the first of the next) are a transition: change habits gradually rather than abruptly.
The six seasons describe the climate of north India. In other regions and hemispheres, match the guidance to local weather (hot-dry, rainy, cold) rather than to calendar months.

items.title: Nidra
items.summary: Sleep is one of the three supports of life (Trayopastambha) with food and regulated sexual life. Good sleep is said to bring happiness, strength, fertility, knowledge and long life.

list: Sleep at night; avoid daytime sleep except in summer or for the weak, elderly, children and those exhausted
Night waking is said to increase Vata and dryness; daytime sleep to increase Kapha and heaviness
For poor sleep: oil massage of head and feet, warm milk, a calm mind before bed

p: Adults generally need 7–9 hours. Persistent insomnia, loud snoring with pauses in breathing, or excessive daytime sleepiness should be assessed by a doctor (for example for sleep apnoea, depression or thyroid disease). Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first-line treatment.

items.title: Vega Dharana
items.summary: Charaka lists thirteen natural urges that must not be suppressed, and mental impulses that should be restrained.

list: Flatus
Faeces
Urine
Sneezing
Thirst
Hunger
Sleep
Cough
Breathlessness after exertion
Yawning
Tears
Vomiting
Semen

p: Greed, grief, fear, anger, vanity, shamelessness, jealousy, excessive attachment and malice; and harmful speech and actions.
Habitual holding of stool or urine is linked to constipation and urinary problems. Forcing urges (for example, inducing vomiting or straining at stool) is equally harmful.

items.title: Swasthavritta
items.summary: Swasthavritta is the Ayurvedic discipline of staying healthy: daily and seasonal routine, ethical conduct (Sadvritta), hygiene, diet and Rasayana.

list: Dinacharya and Ritucharya
Sadvritta: ethical, social and personal conduct
Achara Rasayana: truthfulness, non-violence, compassion and calm as 'rejuvenation'
Ahara: wholesome diet
Yoga and moderate exercise
Blood pressure check at least yearly in adults
Blood sugar screening, especially with family history or excess weight
Cancer screening appropriate to age and sex (cervical, breast, colorectal)
Vaccinations according to the national schedule
Stopping tobacco and limiting alcohol

items.title: Yoga, pranayama and meditation
items.summary: Yoga is a related but separate tradition. Postures, breathing practices and meditation are used alongside Ayurvedic treatment for general wellbeing.

p: Systematic reviews report modest benefits of yoga for chronic low back pain, stress and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life in several chronic conditions. Evidence for disease-specific claims is weaker.

list: Learn from a qualified teacher
Avoid forceful breathing (Kapalabhati, Bhastrika) and breath-holding in pregnancy, heart disease, high blood pressure, epilepsy and after recent surgery
Avoid inversions with glaucoma, uncontrolled blood pressure or neck problems
Stop for pain, dizziness or breathlessness

p: See the Yoga & breathing module for individual practices with cautions.

items.title: Women's health
items.summary: Classical gynaecology (Stri Roga) describes menstrual, uterine and vaginal disorders, with menstruation viewed as a natural monthly cleansing.

list: Artava: menstrual blood, considered an Upadhatu (secondary tissue) of Rasa
Rituchakra: the menstrual cycle, divided into the menstrual phase (Rajasrava Kala), proliferative phase (Ritu Kala) and the post-ovulatory phase (Ritu Vyatita Kala)
Twenty gynaecological disorders (Yonivyapad) described by Charaka and Sushruta

p: Classical texts prescribe rest and dietary restrictions during menstruation. Modern understanding does not support isolation or restrictions on normal activities; rest and comfort as needed are reasonable. Menstruation is not impure.

list: Very heavy bleeding (soaking a pad or tampon every hour for several hours), or bleeding between periods or after sex
Any bleeding after menopause
Severe pelvic pain, or pain with fever
Missed periods with a possible pregnancy
A lump in the breast

p: Classically described as Rajonivritti, a natural transition associated with increasing Vata. Hot flushes, sleep disturbance, mood changes and bone loss can be managed with lifestyle measures and, where suitable, menopausal hormone therapy; discuss bone density and cardiovascular risk with a doctor.

items.title: Pregnancy care (Garbhini Paricharya)
items.summary: Classical texts describe a month-by-month diet and conduct for pregnancy, centred on milk, ghee and nourishing food. Modern antenatal care comes first.

list: Register for antenatal care early and attend all visits and scans
Folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy; iron and calcium as advised
Do not take any herbal, Rasa or Bhasma medicine in pregnancy unless your obstetrician has approved it
Avoid alcohol, tobacco and unpasteurised products

p: Charaka, Sushruta and Vagbhata describe a different diet for each month: for example, cold milk in the first month, milk processed with sweet herbs in the second and third, and ghee and rice preparations in later months; with enemas (Anuvasana Basti) in the eighth and ninth months in classical practice. The procedures in late pregnancy are not recommended without specialist obstetric supervision.
Texts advise a calm, pleasant environment, avoiding heavy exertion, long journeys on rough roads, fasting, sleeping on the back, suppressing urges and frightening experiences.

list: Vaginal bleeding or leaking fluid
Severe headache, blurred vision or swelling of face and hands
Reduced baby movements
Severe abdominal pain, fever or fits

items.title: Postpartum care (Sutika Paricharya)
items.summary: The postpartum woman (Sutika) is considered weak and Vata-aggravated. Classical care uses rest, oil massage, warm baths and digestible, nourishing food for about six weeks.

list: Abhyanga with warm oil and warm water baths
Binding of the abdomen
Light, warm, easily digested food at first, then gradually nourishing food
Avoiding exertion, cold exposure and sexual intercourse during the Sutika period

p: Classical texts describe galactagogue foods and herbs such as Shatavari. Exclusive breastfeeding for about six months is the modern recommendation. Check any herb with your doctor while breastfeeding.

list: Heavy bleeding, large clots or feeling faint
Fever, foul-smelling discharge or a red, painful breast
Calf pain or breathlessness
Low mood, anxiety or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby

items.title: Children's health (Kaumarabhritya)
items.summary: Kaumarabhritya covers newborn care, nutrition, growth and childhood illness. Kashyapa Samhita is its main classical text.

list: Follow the national immunisation schedule; no traditional practice replaces vaccination
Exclusive breastfeeding for about six months, then complementary foods
Regular growth and development checks
Do not give adult Ayurvedic medicines, Rasa preparations or Bhasmas to children

p: A preparation containing processed gold with ghee and honey, promoted for immunity and intellect in children. Its classical basis is a passage in Kashyapa Samhita on Swarna Prashana. There is no robust clinical evidence of benefit, the gold content of products varies, and honey must not be given to infants under one year (risk of infant botulism). It is not a vaccine.

list: Any fever in a baby under 3 months
Fast or difficult breathing, blue lips
Drowsiness, floppiness or a fit
Not feeding, few wet nappies, sunken eyes
A rash that does not fade when pressed

items.title: Men's health
items.summary: Vajikarana covers sexual health, vigour and fertility. Several common men's problems can be signs of other illness and need medical assessment.

p: Vajikarana uses nourishing diet, conduct and drugs (for example Ashwagandha, Shatavari, Kapikacchu, Gokshura) after the body has been cleansed, and emphasises emotional wellbeing and a healthy relationship.

list: Erectile difficulty can be an early sign of heart disease or diabetes: check blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol
Infertility needs semen analysis and assessment of both partners
Urinary hesitancy or weak stream after 50 may be prostate enlargement; blood in urine needs urgent assessment
Many 'herbal' sexual-enhancement products sold online have been found to contain hidden prescription drugs such as sildenafil; avoid unlicensed products

items.title: Healthy ageing (Jara and Rasayana)
items.summary: Old age (Jara) is described as a Vata-predominant stage. Rasayana aims to slow decline and preserve strength, memory and immunity.

list: Regular routine, oil massage, warm and nourishing food
Rasayana drugs such as Amalaki, Haritaki, Guduchi and Chyawanprash, under supervision
Achara Rasayana: calm, ethical and engaged living
Review all medicines and supplements with a doctor or pharmacist at least yearly (risk of interactions)
Prevent falls: strength and balance exercise, good lighting, eye checks
Screen for hearing loss, memory problems, depression and osteoporosis
Kidney and liver function decline with age: doses that suit younger adults may be too high

items.title: Mental health (Manas)
items.summary: Ayurveda describes the mind (Manas) with three qualities, Sattva, Rajas and Tamas, and recognises mental disorders such as Unmada (psychosis-like states) and Apasmara (seizure disorders).

list: Sattva (clarity), Rajas (activity, passion), Tamas (inertia): disorders arise from excess Rajas and Tamas
Medhya Rasayana: herbs said to support intellect, including Mandukaparni, Yashtimadhu, Guduchi and Shankhapushpi
Sattvavajaya Chikitsa: control of the mind by knowledge, courage, memory and concentration, a classical form of psychological therapy
Achara Rasayana: ethical, compassionate conduct
Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, psychosis and epilepsy are treatable with psychological therapies and medicines
Never stop psychiatric or antiepileptic medicines without your doctor, even when feeling better
Herbs such as Ashwagandha, Jatamansi and Brahmi can interact with sedatives and other medicines

p: If you are thinking about harming yourself or ending your life, contact local emergency services or a crisis helpline now (in India, Tele-MANAS: 14416; in the US, 988), or go to the nearest emergency department.

items.title: Agada Tantra
items.summary: Agada Tantra deals with poisons from plants, minerals and animals, and their management. Today, suspected poisoning is a medical emergency.

list: Sthavara Visha: poisons from plants and minerals
Jangama Visha: poisons from animals (snakes, scorpions, insects)
Gara Visha: artificial or combined poisons
Dushi Visha: weak, residual poison that persists in the body

p: For any suspected poisoning, call emergency services or a poison centre immediately. Do not induce vomiting unless a medical professional tells you to. Take the container or plant to hospital.

items.title: Snakebite: first aid
items.summary: Snakebite needs urgent hospital care with antivenom. Traditional remedies must never delay transport.

list: Keep calm and keep the person still
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing from the bitten limb
Immobilise the limb with a splint, at about heart level
Get to a hospital with antivenom as fast as possible
Note the time of the bite and any symptoms
Cut, suck or burn the wound
Apply a tight tourniquet
Apply herbs, chemicals or ice
Wait for symptoms to appear before going to hospital
Try to catch or kill the snake

sources.text: World Health Organization guidance on snakebite envenoming

items.title: Poisonous medicinal plants
items.summary: Several plants used in Ayurvedic pharmacy are poisonous in their raw form and are used only after purification (Shodhana) in tiny doses by trained physicians.

head: Plant
Botanical name
Main danger
rows: Heart rhythm disturbance, death; one of the most toxic
Confusion, delirium, fast heart rate, high temperature
Abrin: vomiting, organ failure if seeds are chewed
Latex burns eyes and skin; cardiac effects

p: Never prepare or take these at home. Keep products containing them away from children. Formulation pages in this encyclopedia mark preparations containing toxic herbs.

items.title: Heavy metals in herbal products
items.summary: Some Ayurvedic preparations intentionally contain processed metals and minerals; contamination also occurs. Lead, mercury and arsenic poisoning have been reported.

p: A study of Ayurvedic products bought online in the United States found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in about one in five products, and more often in Rasa Shastra products (Saper RB et al., JAMA 2008). Cases of lead poisoning linked to Ayurvedic medicines have been reported repeatedly in medical journals.

list: Take mineral preparations only when prescribed, for the shortest time
Buy only from licensed GMP manufacturers; ask for heavy-metal test reports
Never give such products to children or in pregnancy without specialist advice
Tell your doctor about any such product; blood lead testing is simple
Abdominal pain, constipation
Tiredness, anaemia
Headache, memory problems, irritability
Tingling or weakness in hands and feet

sources.text: Saper RB et al. Lead, mercury, and arsenic in US- and Indian-manufactured Ayurvedic medicines sold via the Internet. JAMA 2008;300(8):915–923

items.title: Reading the evidence
items.english: How to judge whether a treatment works
items.summary: A classical reference shows that a treatment was used traditionally. Whether it works and is safe is a separate question, answered by well-designed human studies.

list: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials
Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) with adequate size and blinding
Controlled studies without randomisation
Cohort and case-control studies
Case series and case reports
Laboratory and animal studies (cannot show benefit in people)
Expert opinion and traditional texts

sections.h: Questions to ask of any study
list: Who took part, and are they like me?
What was the comparison: placebo, standard treatment or nothing?
Was it randomised and blinded?
Were the outcomes important ones (symptoms, complications, survival) rather than only lab values?
How large was the effect, and how many people had side effects?
Has it been repeated by independent groups?

p: Condition articles give a separate clinical-evidence rating: some, limited or very limited. A rating describes human study evidence only and never the authority of the classical text.

items.title: Research highlights and institutions
items.summary: Research capacity has grown through government councils and universities, but most clinical studies remain small. Some areas have stronger evidence than others.

list: Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS), Ministry of Ayush: clinical research, drug standardisation and literary research
All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi
Institute of Teaching and Research in Ayurveda, Jamnagar
National Pharmacovigilance Programme for Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs: reporting of adverse reactions
Kshara Sutra for fistula-in-ano: an ICMR-supported multicentre randomised trial compared it with conventional surgery (Indian Journal of Medical Research, 1991)
Yoga for chronic low back pain: several systematic reviews report modest benefit
Small sample sizes and short follow-up
Lack of blinding or proper control groups
Variation in formulations between manufacturers
Few independent replications and limited safety reporting

p: If you suspect a reaction to an Ayurvedic medicine, tell your doctor and report it through the national pharmacovigilance programme or your country's medicines regulator.
